articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. This action targets entities involved in intellectual property theft and illicit activities that undermine U.S. economic interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses aim to provide guidance and authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, ensuring that legitimate activities are not unduly impacted by the new sanctions.
The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating intellectual property theft and protecting American innovation on a global scale.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License on October 16, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning certain activities involving Venezuela.
Alongside the amended General License, OFAC also published a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) to provide further clarity and guidance on the scope and application of the updated regulations.
The changes reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela, aiming to balance humanitarian concerns with pressure on the Maduro regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities deemed to be supporting illicit activities in both regions.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions. These documents aim to clarify the scope of the new sanctions and provide guidance for compliance.

The Iran-related designations are part of the ongoing U.S. effort to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities, while the Cuba designation reinforces existing sanctions against the Cuban government.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Entity from Venezuela-Related Designations List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of an entity from its Venezuela-related designations list on October 14, 2026. This action signifies a de-escalation of sanctions against a specific party previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.

Designation removals by OFAC typically occur when the designated party demonstrates a change in behavior or when the U.S. government determines that the basis for the original designation no longer applies.
This removal may indicate a shift in policy regarding certain Venezuelan entities or a response to specific actions taken by the delisted party to address U.S. concerns.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in international drug trafficking and terrorism financing networks.

These actions aim to disrupt the financial infrastructure of criminal organizations and terrorist groups, preventing them from accessing the U.S. financial system and limiting their ability to operate globally.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating illicit activities that pose a threat to national security and international stability.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court Official, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026, for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This settlement highlights OFAC's continued enforcement efforts against companies that fail to comply with U.S. sanctions laws.

In a separate action, OFAC designated an official of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses. This designation reflects U.S. policy concerns regarding the ICC's actions.
Additionally, OFAC announced the removal of a Burma-related designation, indicating a potential shift in U.S. policy or a response to developments in Burma.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license authorizes certain transactions and activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs.
General Licenses are often issued to facilitate humanitarian aid, ensure the flow of certain essential goods, or to carve out specific activities from broader sanctions regimes.
This new General License reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions strategy concerning Russia, potentially in response to evolving geopolitical or economic considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran-Related General License and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security interests.

Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License, which may authorize certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited. Additionally, an existing Russia-related General License was amended, indicating adjustments to the scope of authorized activities concerning Russia.
These actions demonstrate the U.S. government's dynamic approach to sanctions, continuously adapting to evolving threats and geopolitical landscapes in both Iran and Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates on October 5, 2026. These actions reflect ongoing reviews of sanctions lists and adjustments based on new information or changes in circumstances.

In addition to the list updates, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert, providing guidance and warnings regarding potential sanctions evasion tactics or high-risk activities involving Iran. An amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) was also released to offer further clarification on existing regulations.
These measures aim to enhance the effectiveness of sanctions programs while ensuring that the public and regulated entities have the most current information for compliance.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., imposing a civil penalty of $11,662,930.
The penalty addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

OFAC's enforcement release found 475 apparent violations, totaling approximately $14.8 million, from September 2021 to April 2025. These violations included 403 payments, amounting to $14.3 million, sent to or through 35 blocked banks.

This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations by Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. The specific details of the violations were not immediately released but typically involve transactions with sanctioned entities or in sanctioned jurisdictions.
OFAC continues to emphasize the importance of robust compliance programs for all entities engaged in international trade and logistics to prevent sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations

While the specific details of the individual's violations were not immediately disclosed, OFAC frequently pursues enforcement actions against individuals who engage in unauthorized transactions with sanctioned countries or entities.
This penalty serves as a reminder that sanctions compliance obligations extend to individuals, not just corporations, and that significant financial consequences can result from non-compliance.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a historic $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread breakdowns in its Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program.
This penalty, the largest in OCC history, comes nearly two years after the bank signed a cease-and-desist order in December 2024, committing to address its longstanding BSA deficiencies.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould stated that the bank's 'poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable' and that its BSA/AML compliance program 'continues to reflect widespread breakdowns in internal controls, which threatens U.S. national and economic security.'

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express on October 8, 2026. This action was taken due to significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs.
The OCC found that American Express's BSA/AML program suffered from systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training.

These deficiencies included a BSA/AML risk assessment that did not sufficiently address the risks associated with its credit and charge-card business, and a failure to maintain an effective framework for ongoing customer due diligence.

articles.headline: BIS Adds 29 Entries to Entity List, Citing National Security Concerns
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 29 entries to the Entity List, effective October 8, 2026. These additions include 26 entities and 3 addresses under the destinations of the People's Republic of China (19), Turkey (9), and the United Arab Emirates (1).

These entities have been determined by the U.S. Government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States. The Entity List imposes additional license requirements and limits the availability of most license exceptions for exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) when a listed entity is a party to the transaction.
BIS also warned that exporters need to exercise due diligence to ensure items are not being diverted to prohibited end-uses or end-users, beyond just screening against the Entity List.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
